comments.author: @pmiddlet72
comments.text:
One key issue I see with OpenAI's discussions on fine-tuning models and their implications for organizations of any size is what Wes pointed out—the 'I am Death' problem. Looking ahead to the GenAI landscape by the end of 2025 or 2026, we might witness a consolidation of power among major AI players, potentially labeled as 'Big AI.' This could lead to the displacement of smaller startups or the absorption of their niche applications through partnerships with larger corporations, resulting in significant challenges for smaller entities to compete at the same pace.

While the concept of last-mover advantage sounds appealing, the reality is that the future landscape of AI models remains uncertain. Base models are proprietary, and insights into their development are typically disclosed by major players close to their release. Consequently, access to these advancements may predominantly favor larger companies through partnerships, further hindering smaller players' ability to innovate in niche spaces due to the high costs associated with legal intellectual property (IP).

Furthermore, the deployment, profitability, and sustainability of AI-driven products are heavily influenced by the decisions of well-funded corporations, potentially leaving smaller companies scrambling for any remaining opportunities to stay afloat. For instance, the recent releases of Devin AI and AutoDev raise questions about which companies, small or large, are being courted, and how pricing structures will impact smaller players disproportionately unless there's a commitment to inclusivity in pricing.

In essence, while the notion of AI democratization sounds promising, the reality may involve significant challenges for smaller entities to compete on equal footing. It's essential for stakeholders, including OpenAI, to consider these dynamics seriously when discussing the future of AI.

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
The layers approach you described makes little sense to me.

There are two ways to go about making layers on top of the base.

The obvious way is to train the LLM using your specific data, hoping to enhance functionality.

That won't work. OpenAI does not share base training data. So if you start twiddling weights, you will be overwriting existing weights. You can't help but degrade the original functionality. To optimize, you have to retrain all of the model using original data plus the added specialized data.

Besides, training is expensive in compute cycles. LLMs really can only be trained by giant data centers with big energy budgets.

That combined insight comes from Andrej Karpathy.

The alternative is to preserve the original LLM weights and slap a front-end on it consisting of UI + canned, tested queries. This is easy and cheap. You don't need a kazillion compute cycles. It's laptop at the beach work.

But then the model won't gain optimized weights for your particular application. It might be a little better than the vanilla model. But how much could you charge for that? Eventually folks will start sharing optimized queries for free. It's not that hard.

Conceptually, optimizing queries is something many folks are already familiar with. They do it for search engine queries. Would you pay someone to optimize your search queries for you? I think most will not.

For serious app functionality enhancement, you'll have to give your training data to OpenAI and pay them to retrain the whole freakin' model, just for you.

I'm not seeing how this layers thing turns into value without a massive budget and contracting with OpenAI to retrain the model using your additional data.
